title: Sealed replay and scoring
bridge: A sealed replay is like a Playwright test with a mocked API. Byte asks its usual questions, and a fake answers from a fixed file. Except the fake is Byte's real broker with no token, and the checkout has no history and no route out. So Byte cannot peek at what happened after the PR.
intro: BYTE-GOLD only means something if Byte reviews each old PR the way it would have back then. This lesson packs a case and replays it through the real worker image on a sealed network. A judge then scores the findings. Then it makes that score a required check in RhinoHealth/byte.

picture.caption: One case goes from byte-gold to a number the gate can compare.

steps.text: gold-pack fetches the two SHAs and the PR metadata with a read-only token
broker --replay /input serves Byte's gh reads from the pack
asks for the diff and the files, exactly as in production
the only way out: HTTPS to api.anthropic.com
recall by severity and clean alarms, compared with the main baseline

sections.h: Open one case and pack it
p: Take `cases/real-0042` from lesson g2-1 and run `byte gold-pack --case cases/real-0042 --fcp ~/src/fcp --out packs/real-0042`. A pack is a folder with everything Byte needs to review that PR and nothing else. It has three files under `input/`.

`pr.json` holds the title, the body unless `blankBody` is set, the files with additions and deletions, the refs and SHAs. They come from `gh api repos/RhinoHealth/fcp/pulls/<n>` and `/files`. It also holds `reviewArgs`: the flags Byte's gate would pass for fcp, so the replay runs the same way as production.

`diff.patch` is `git diff <base>...<head>`, with `planted.patch` appended for a planted case. `tree.tar` is `git archive <head>` with the patch applied: the files at the head commit and no `.git` folder. A shallow fetch of the two SHAs is enough; nobody needs the full history.

Why so careful? SWE-bench agents were caught reading future git history and finding the fix. A tree with no `.git` and a broker with no token close that path. The code lives in `src/gold.ts` as `goldPack()`, wired into `src/cli.ts` in the same `argsToMap` and `required` style as the other subcommands.

callout.text: Byte must review the old PR as it would have back then. Anything that happened after the merge, the fix, the comments, the revert, is a leak.

sections.h: The replay broker, part 1: a session with no token
p: In production Byte's worker never calls GitHub itself. It asks the broker, which holds the token and answers only reads about the one PR (Byte's `src/broker.ts`). A replay broker is the same `BrokerSession` class, but its answers come from the pack. The worker runs unchanged and cannot tell the difference.

The sketch is 33 lines, so it comes in two blocks; nothing is removed between them. First, give `BrokerSessionOptions` in `src/broker.ts` an optional `api` next to the existing `executeRead` injection. Then `src/gold-broker.ts` builds a session with both injected.
sections.because: Byte's worker only ever talks to a broker, so a broker that answers from the pack lets the worker run unchanged.

notes.text: Promise-based file reads and writes from Node; no extra library.
The real, security-reviewed BrokerSession and the result type its reads return. We reuse it, we do not copy it.
The command that starts it: `byte broker --replay /input`. No token, no network; the review and comment listings are empty.
One function: where the pack is, where to write results, and the capability, the per-run bearer the worker must present.
pr.json parsed into a ReplayPr, a small type you declare in this file for the pack's shape.
The diff as one string, read once. Every `gh pr diff` call gets this exact text.
A helper that wraps text as a successful command result: exit code 0, the text on stdout, nothing on stderr.
A list of everything Byte tries to publish. It grows as the review runs.
A real BrokerSession; everything below is its options.
The session is hard-scoped to one repository, PR number and head SHA, as in production. Reads about anything else are refused.
An empty token. There is nothing to leak, because both GitHub paths, reads and writes, are injected below.
The secret guard list: the capability must never appear in anything the broker passes on.

sections.h: The replay broker, part 2: reads and publications
p: The second block, lines 19 to 33, injects the two GitHub paths. `executeRead` gets the `gh` argument list the worker sent and returns a result. `api` receives what Byte would post as a review and records it instead.

`pick`, `jsonFields`, `recordingApi` and `ReplayPr` are small helpers the sketch assumes in this file; you write them. `jsonFields` reads the `--json` field list out of a `gh pr view` call, `pick` keeps only those fields. `/v1/head` always says unchanged, so the head-SHA re-check before writes passes.

Tests go in `test/gold-broker.test.ts`, run with `node --test` via tsx. They check that `gh pr diff` returns the pack's patch and that an unknown endpoint is refused. They also check that a publication lands in the file and that nothing touches the network.
sections.because: Every replay is a first review, so earlier reviews and comments must come back empty, and unknown reads are refused.

notes.text: The injected read: `args` is the gh argument list, for example ["pr", "diff", "12"].
`gh pr diff` gets the pack's diff. In production this is the one read Byte makes on every review.
`gh pr view --json title,body,...` gets only the fields it asked for, from the pack's view object.
`gh api repos/.../pulls/<n>/files` gets the files list with additions and deletions.
Reviews and comments listings return `[]`. Every replay is a first review; later comments would be a leak.
Anything else: exit code 1 and a reason. The broker's audit records refused reads, which the smoke test checks.
The new injection: a recording API. It receives each review Byte would post.
Keep it in memory, so the file always holds every publication of the run.
Write `publication.json` into the output folder. gold-score reads this file later.
Return an id like GitHub would, so the worker's code path stays the same.

sections.ifInstead: If instead the worker logs `not in the replay pack` for a production read, answer it from the pack in executeRead. Never give the broker a token.

p: `scripts/gold-replay.sh <pack> <image> <out>` replays one pack through the real Byte worker image. It reuses review.yml's container pattern. A per-run network, a capability from `openssl rand -hex 32`, and `--cap-drop ALL --read-only --security-opt no-new-privileges` on every container.
The script is 29 lines, so it comes in two blocks; nothing is removed between them. Part 1 is setup: names, the capability, a temp folder for the tree, and a trap that cleans up whatever happens.
sections.because: Each replay gets its own network, capability and temp tree, so two runs never share anything and the trap always cleans up.

code.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/gold-replay.sh <pack> <worker image> <out>: one BYTE-GOLD case, sealed.
# The worker sees the tree (no .git), the replay broker (no token) and one host
# out. The answer key is never mounted anywhere. SQUID_IMAGE is digest-pinned.
set -euo pipefail
pack="$1"; image="$2"; out="$3"
id="$(jq -r .id "$pack/input/pr.json")"
net="gold-$id-$$"; cap="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"; tree="$(mktemp -d)"
mapfile -t review_args < <(jq -r '.reviewArgs[]' "$pack/input/pr.json") # what the gate would pass for fcp
trap 'docker rm -f "gb-$id" "ge-$id" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true; docker network rm "$net" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true; rm -rf "$tree"' EXIT
tar -xf "$pack/input/tree.tar" -C "$tree"
mkdir -p "$out/$id"

notes.text: What the script does, in one line. The three arguments: the pack folder, the worker image, the output folder.
The rule of the script: no answer key is ever mounted. The squid image is pinned by digest, like every third-party image.
Stop on any error, on an unset variable, and on a failure inside a pipe. Standard for every bash script in Byte.
The case id, read from pr.json with jq. It names the containers and the output folder.
A network name unique to this run, a fresh capability, and a temp folder for the tree. `$$` is the shell's process id.
mapfile reads the reviewArgs array from pr.json into a bash array, one flag per element. These are the flags the gate would pass for fcp.
The trap runs on exit, success or failure: remove both containers, remove the network, delete the temp tree.
Unpack tree.tar into the temp folder. This is the checkout the worker will see: files only, no .git.
One output folder per case: publication.json, claude-result.json and run-manifest.json land here.

p: Part 2, lines 13 to 29, starts three containers on one internal network. An internal Docker network has no route out: a container on it cannot reach the internet or the laptop's other networks. The lab shows this with one curl.

The only exception is squid, the egress proxy from lesson p4-5. It sits on the internal network and on the default bridge, so it can reach out. Its config allows one host: `api.anthropic.com`. `config/gold-squid.conf` reuses the allow-list lines from infrastructure's `modules/squid-proxy` template, without the basic auth.
Never mount byte-gold or the answers. Replays talk to Claude directly, like live Byte reviews; Byte does not use the gateway.
Smoke-test 5 packs on byte-runner-set and check three things. Squid's log shows only api.anthropic.com. The broker's audit shows no refused reads. The manifest has the same shape as a live review's.
sections.because: The worker may reach only the broker and Claude, so one internal network plus one proxy is the whole sandbox.

code.text:
docker network create --internal "$net" >/dev/null # no route out
docker run -d --name "ge-$id" --network "$net" --read-only --tmpfs /var/spool/squid --tmpfs /var/run \
  -v "$PWD/config/gold-squid.conf:/etc/squid/squid.conf:ro" "$SQUID_IMAGE" >/dev/null # allows api.anthropic.com only
docker network connect bridge "ge-$id" # the one container with a way out
docker run -d --name "gb-$id" --network "$net" --cap-drop ALL --read-only --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  -e BYTE_BROKER_CAPABILITY="$cap" -v "$pack/input:/input:ro" -v "$out/$id:/output" \
  "$image" broker --replay /input >/dev/null
# (wait for the broker's /health as review.yml does)

docker run --rm --network "$net" --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" --cap-drop ALL --read-only \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,nodev,size=256m -e HOME=/tmp/byte-home \
  -e HTTPS_PROXY="http://ge-$id:3128" -e CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1 -e CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN \
  -e BYTE_BROKER_URL="http://gb-$id:8080" -e BYTE_BROKER_CAPABILITY="$cap" \
  -v "$tree:/workspace:ro" -v "$out/$id:/output" -w /workspace \
  "$image" review "${review_args[@]}" --check-id 0 --output-directory /output \
  > "$out/$id/runner-result.json" 2> "$out/$id/runner-stderr.log"

notes.text: `--internal`: Docker gives this network no route out. Nothing on it can reach the internet by itself.
The squid container, read-only, with tmpfs for its spool and run folders because it must write somewhere.
Its config is mounted read-only from the repo. SQUID_IMAGE is the digest-pinned image, passed in the environment.
The one line that gives a way out: squid also joins the default bridge network. Only squid, never the worker.
The replay broker: capabilities dropped, read-only, no privilege escalation. The same flags review.yml uses.
It gets the capability, the pack's input folder read-only, and the output folder. No BYTE_BROKER_TOKEN at all.
`broker --replay /input` starts the session from part 1 of the broker.
Wait for GET /health before starting the worker, the way review.yml does.
The worker runs as your user id, with capabilities dropped and a read-only root file system.
A small tmpfs for /tmp with noexec, and HOME inside it. Claude Code gets a writable home that disappears after the run.
HTTPS_PROXY points at squid on port 3128. CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC stops Claude Code's non-essential calls, such as update checks, which squid would refuse anyway.
The broker URL and the capability, the same two variables the production worker gets.
The unpacked tree mounted read-only at /workspace, the output folder, and the working directory set to the tree.
`review` with the pack's reviewArgs, a check id of 0 because there is no GitHub check run, and the output folder.
The worker's JSON result and its stderr, kept per case next to publication.json.

callout.text: One fresh network and tree per run. The answer key is never mounted. The only host out is api.anthropic.com, and only squid can reach it.

sections.h: Scoring, part 1: the window and the judge
p: `byte gold-score --cases <byte-gold> --results <dir> --output <file>` reads every case and its `publication.json`, and matches Byte's findings to the golden comments. Matching has two stages. First a filter in code. A finding can only match a golden comment on the same path, within 10 lines of its range.

Only those pairs go to the judge. The judge is a small Claude call: `claude -p --model claude-haiku-5-5 --effort low`, with no tools and JSON out. It answers one question: does this finding describe this defect? It reuses the session flags and token handling of `weekly-analyze`. This is the Uber and Martian method: a model matches comments, code keeps it cheap and strict.

Before the gate trusts the judge, Sean and Nave label 50 pairs by hand and compare. Below 90% agreement, switch the judge to Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort and check again. The sketch is 33 lines, so it comes in two blocks; nothing is removed between them.
sections.because: A location filter in code keeps the judge cheap and strict: only findings near a golden comment are ever asked about.

notes.text: Byte's finding type from review.ts: path, line, severity and body. Only the type is imported.
A golden comment, the same shape as the `golden` entries in case.json from lesson g2-1.
A case with its split: `dev` cases run on every gated PR, `holdout` cases once a month.
The judge is a function type that returns a Promise of true or false. Tests pass a fake; production passes the Claude call.
The model choice and its condition, written next to the code so nobody forgets the calibration step.
Haiku 5.5 at low effort for a yes/no question. Cheap, and the filter already removed the hard cases.
The window: 10 lines above the golden start line and 10 below its end line.
`near` is the filter: same path, and the finding's line inside the widened range. Nothing else reaches the judge.

p: Part 2, lines 15 to 33, scores one case. Recall is the share of golden bugs Byte caught. Precision is the share of Byte's findings that matched a golden bug, counted over real and planted cases. A false alarm is a high or medium finding on a clean case.

The scorecard reports per split, team and kind. It has recall for high, medium and low golden bugs, precision, and high or medium findings per clean PR. It also has the API-equivalent cost and minutes per review, from `claude-result.json`. Numbers only, like `data/runs.jsonl`: no path, code or finding text. The JSON goes to the G1 eval store and a markdown table to the job summary.
sections.because: Only numbers leave this function, so the scorecard can be stored and shown without ever carrying a golden comment out of byte-gold.

notes.text: One case, Byte's findings from its publication.json, and a judge. Async because the judge is a model call.
Findings already matched, so one finding can never count for two golden comments.
The per-golden result: its severity and whether it was caught. Recall by severity comes from this list.
Walk the golden comments one by one.
Only unmatched findings that pass `near` are candidates for this golden comment.
Ask the judge. On the first yes, mark the finding, count the bug as caught, and stop looking.
Record the outcome for this golden comment, caught or not.
Alarms are findings that are not low. A missing severity ranks as high, the same rule Byte uses when posting.
Ids and enums from the case, then the per-golden list.
How many findings matched. Precision across cases is matched over total findings.
Only clean cases report alarms. The pass bar is a mean of at most 0.2 per clean PR; real and planted cases get null here.

sections.h: gold.yml, part 1: when the gate runs
p: Today every Byte change ships on review alone, and a merge to main repins the whole fleet within minutes. `.github/workflows/gold.yml` makes quality measurable before that. It is the gate from the picture. A required check on byte's main replays the dev split and fails when quality drops.

The sketch is 34 lines, so it comes in two blocks; nothing is removed between them. Part 1 says when the job runs and under what rules. Splits are assigned once in byte-gold by a stable hash of the case id, two thirds dev and one third holdout. The hash is stratified, which means balanced, by kind, team and severity. Only Sean and Nave see per-case holdout results.
sections.because: Only changes that can move Byte's quality should pay for a replay, and the merged result must become the new baseline.

code.text:
name: BYTE-GOLD
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["skills/**", "src/engines.ts", "src/limits.ts", "src/review.ts", "src/panel.ts", "config/repositories.json", "Dockerfile"]
  push: # the merged result becomes the baseline row in data/gold-runs.jsonl
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["skills/**", "src/engines.ts", "src/limits.ts", "src/review.ts", "src/panel.ts", "config/repositories.json", "Dockerfile"]
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 19 1 * *" # holdout split, monthly, in the evening
permissions:
  contents: read
concurrency:
  group: byte-gold-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true # only a PR's newest head is worth scoring
jobs:
  gold:
    # Byte's own fix PRs are opened by the App: model-written code never runs next to the answer key.
    if: github.event_name != 'pull_request' || github.event.pull_request.user.type != 'Bot'
    runs-on: byte-runner-set

notes.text: On pull requests, but only when the listed paths change.
The paths that can move quality: playbooks, the engine, limits, review, the panel, policy, and the Dockerfile because it pins Claude Code.
The same paths on main. The merged result becomes the baseline row in data/gold-runs.jsonl on the telemetry branch.
The first of each month at 19:00 UTC, the holdout split. Evening, so it does not compete with live reviews for quota.
The job's own GITHUB_TOKEN can only read. The fcp read token and the byte-gold key come from the steps in part 2.
One run per PR at a time, keyed by PR number, or by ref on main and schedule.
A new push cancels the running replay: only a PR's newest head is worth scoring.
Skip PRs opened by a Bot. Byte's own fix PRs are opened by the App, and model-written code must never run next to the answer key.
byte-runner-set: the same single-use runners as live reviews, so the score describes what ships.

sections.h: gold.yml, part 2: the steps and the pass bar
p: Part 2, lines 20 to 34, is the job's steps. `scripts/gold-run.sh` does the work in order: leak check, pack, replay, score, pass bar. The leak check fails first if any case's PR number, head SHA or Jira key appears under `skills/`. The weekly loop writes MEMORY.md from live findings, so it could copy a case in by accident.

Packs are cached by case id and built with the read-only App token; the token never enters a container. Replays run 4 at a time against the image built from the PR. Scope follows the change: a PR under `skills/<team>/` replays only that team's cases, so the weekly MEMORY.md PRs stay cheap. Engine, limits, review, panel, policy or Dockerfile changes replay every dev case.
The pass bar has two parts. HIGH recall at most 3 points below the latest main row in `data/gold-runs.jsonl`. And at most 0.2 high or medium findings per clean PR.

Run main 3 times first to measure noise. If runs differ by more than 3 points, re-run only the cases that flipped. Replays share Byte's Claude quota with live reviews; if live reviews start hitting 429s, move runs to the evening.
sections.because: The PR's own image is scored against byte-gold, so a prompt or playbook change must earn its place before it ships.

notes.text: Check out byte at the PR head, pinned by SHA with the version in a comment, as every action in Byte is.
No credentials left in the checkout, so nothing later in the job can push with them.
A second checkout: byte-gold into the `gold` folder. The answer key arrives here, and only here.
An open decision for DevOps: a read-only deploy key, or a small read-only GitHub App for byte-gold.
Mint a GitHub App token for fcp only, so gold-pack can fetch two SHAs per case.
Contents and pull requests, read only. The packs need nothing else.
Build the worker image from the PR, tagged with the commit SHA. Local only: never pushed, so the fleet is never repinned by this job.
GH_TOKEN is the fcp read token for gold-pack. It is used on the runner and never passed to a container.
The Claude token the worker needs, the same secret live reviews use.
The split: holdout on the monthly schedule, dev on every PR and main push.
The whole pipeline in one script, so the lab, the smoke test and CI run exactly the same steps.

callout.text: Agents never change the checks they are judged by. The Bot guard keeps Byte's own PRs out of this job. The paths list means a prompt change cannot skip the gate.

lab.title: Pack, score and seal on your laptop
youNeed: The gold-lab repo from lesson g2-1

worked.do: cd gold-lab && mkdir -p pack/input && git diff "$(git rev-list --max-parents=0 HEAD)...$(git log --format=%h --grep='(#12)')" > pack/input/diff.patch && git archive "$(git log --format=%h --grep='(#12)')" -o pack/input/tree.tar && tar -tf pack/input/tree.tar

git log --format=%H --grep='(#12)' to get the head SHA. Write pack/input/pr.json by hand. Contents: { "id": "real-0001", "repository": "lab/gold-lab", "number": 12, "headSha": "<the full SHA>", "reviewArgs": ["--repository", "lab/gold-lab", "--pr", "12", "--engine", "claude"], "view": { "title": "Shout the greeting", "body": "" }, "files": [{ "filename": "src/greet.ts", "additions": 1, "deletions": 1 }] } Then: jq -r '.reviewArgs[]' pack/input/pr.json

Write the lab's stub src/review.ts, not Byte's real file. One line: export interface ModelFinding { path: string; line: number; severity: "high" | "medium" | "low" | null; body: string }. Copy the two gold-score.ts blocks above, in order, into src/gold-score.ts. Then: ls src

mkdir test and write test/gold-score.test.ts with node:test and node:assert/strict. A fake judge: async (f, g) => f.body.includes("upper-cases") && g.defect.includes("upper-cases"). A real case: golden comment on src/greet.ts lines 2 to 2, severity high, defect "The greeting upper-cases the whole name." Three tests. First: a high finding on src/greet.ts line 5, body "upper-cases every name". Expect golden [{ severity: "high", caught: true }], matchedFindings 1 and cleanAlarms null. Second: the same finding on src/other.ts gives caught false. Third: a clean case with one medium and one low finding gives cleanAlarms 1.

quiz.q: Why does the replay broker answer the reviews and comments listings with []?

options.text: GitHub rate-limits those endpoints, so the pack leaves them out
options.why: The pack never calls them at all; rate limits are not the reason.

options.text: Every replay is a first review, so Byte must not see later comments
options.why: Comments written after the merge, including the fix discussion, would leak the answer.

options.text: The pack would be too big with the comment history
options.why: Size is not the problem; the history is the leak.

quiz.q: Which container in gold-replay.sh has a route out of the internal network?

options.text: squid, which also joins the bridge network and allows only api.anthropic.com
options.why: That one `docker network connect bridge` line is the whole way out, and squid's allow-list has one host.

options.text: The worker, because it must reach Claude
options.why: The worker reaches Claude through HTTPS_PROXY pointing at squid; it has no route of its own.

options.text: The broker, because it must reach GitHub
options.why: The replay broker has no token and answers everything from the pack.

quiz.q: A PR changes only skills/be/MEMORY.md. What does the gate replay?

options.text: Every dev case, because any playbook change can move quality
options.why: That would make the weekly MEMORY.md PRs expensive; scope follows the change.

options.text: Nothing, because MEMORY.md is data, not code
options.why: skills/** is in the paths list; a playbook is part of the prompt.

options.text: Only the BE team's dev cases, after the leak check
options.why: A PR under skills/<team>/ replays that team's cases; engine or policy changes replay every dev case.
